### **Draft – Further Extension Request (Refined & Integrated)**

**Subject: Request for Further Extension for Compliance with Digital Invoicing Requirements under Rules 150Q and 150V of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006**

Dear Sir,

We write on behalf of our above-named client with reference to our earlier correspondence, including the extension request previously submitted and subsequent communications exchanged with your good office in respect of compliance with the mandatory digital invoicing requirements prescribed under Rule 150Q of the Sales Tax Rules, 2006.

At the outset, we remain grateful for the extension earlier granted, which has enabled our client to make substantive progress towards implementation. In continuation thereof, we wish to apprise your good office that the client has now reached the **final stage of contractual arrangements with the approved e-invoicing integration service provider**, and the agreement is presently under execution. The formal signing process is underway and is expected to be completed shortly, following which the client will proceed immediately with system integration, testing, and deployment.

However, it is respectfully submitted that the implementation of digital invoicing within the oil marketing sector is not merely a standalone technical exercise but is intrinsically linked with **industry-wide operational and system alignment challenges**, which are currently under active deliberation at the level of the **Oil Companies Advisory Council (OCAC)**. As also evidenced from the recent correspondence addressed by OCAC to the Federal Board of Revenue, certain critical matters relating to **e-invoicing integration and sales tax return system alignment remain unresolved and require coordinated resolution with FBR and PRAL**. fileciteturn0file1  

In particular, the industry continues to face practical challenges including, inter alia, the absence of system-enabled mechanisms for handling **sales reversals, debit/credit notes, price adjustments, and secondary sales distinctions**, as well as issues relating to **unit of measurement discrepancies (liters vs kilograms), treatment of advances, and reporting of temperature gain/loss adjustments in sales tax returns**. These are not entity-specific issues but systemic constraints, which directly impact the accuracy, reliability, and completeness of digital invoicing and tax reporting.

While our client remains fully committed to FBR’s digitization initiative and has taken all necessary steps within its control, it is evident that **premature implementation in the absence of resolution of these structural issues may lead to inconsistencies between commercial records and tax reporting**, thereby exposing the client to unintended compliance risks.

In parallel, discussions with respective OMCs are ongoing at the OCAC platform, and we understand that **a formal meeting with FBR has already been requested and is expected to be convened shortly to address these matters at an industry level**. The outcome of these discussions will be critical in ensuring a uniform and technically sound implementation framework across the sector.

In view of the above, and considering that (i) contractual finalization is nearing completion, and (ii) key industry-wide issues are under active consideration with FBR, it is respectfully submitted that the present case squarely falls within the scope of **Rule 150V**, which allows extension where compliance is rendered impracticable due to genuine operational and technical constraints.

Accordingly, we humbly request that **further extension up to May 31, 2026** may kindly be granted to our client for completion of digital invoicing integration. We assure your good office that the client will utilize this time exclusively to finalize integration, complete testing, and ensure a smooth and compliant transition to the digital invoicing regime.

We further request that **no adverse or coercive action may be initiated during this interim period**, as the delay is neither deliberate nor due to inaction, but arises from genuine practical constraints coupled with ongoing industry-level coordination with FBR.

We remain fully committed to ensuring timely compliance and will continue to keep your good office apprised of all material developments in this regard.

Your cooperation and continued support in facilitating a smooth transition to the digital invoicing regime is highly appreciated.

Yours sincerely,  

---

### **Practical Note (from experience)**  
A letter structured like this does two important things:

1. **Shifts the narrative from “delay by taxpayer” to “industry-level system readiness”** — which is far stronger legally and practically.  
2. **Creates protection against penal exposure**, especially if later any proceedings are initiated under Rule 150Q non-compliance.

If you want, I can also prepare a **short covering email + annexure list (earlier letters + OCAC correspondence)** to make this submission more defensible at LTO level.

Based on the document you shared, I’ve distilled the most impactful and **public-relevant tax and economic updates** into engaging social media posts. Each post is designed to be **informative, easy to understand, and attention-grabbing**, while still reflecting the real legal and economic implications.

---

### **1. “Fuel Subsidies May End – What It Means for You”**

The IMF has advised Pakistan to gradually phase out fuel subsidies and expand the tax base to ensure long-term fiscal stability. fileciteturn0file0  

From a practical standpoint, this signals two things for the general public and businesses. First, fuel prices may increasingly reflect international market rates, meaning less artificial control and potentially higher volatility in prices. Second, the government may shift towards taxing a broader segment of the economy rather than relying on a limited base.  

For taxpayers, this typically translates into **stricter documentation requirements, increased compliance monitoring, and reduced room for undocumented transactions**. Businesses operating outside the formal system may find it increasingly difficult to remain unnoticed.

---

### **2. “Is Section 7E Tax Unconstitutional? A Major Legal Battle Begins”**

The Federal Constitutional Court is currently examining whether tax under Section 7E—based on deemed rental income of property—is legally valid. fileciteturn0file0  

This provision effectively taxes property owners even when no actual income is earned, by assuming a notional rental value. The core legal challenge is whether the government can tax something that does not exist in real economic terms.  

If the courts ultimately strike down this provision, it could have **significant implications for property owners**, including potential relief from annual tax burdens and even possible refund claims for prior years—subject, of course, to final judgments and procedural limitations.

---

### **3. “Agricultural Income: Federal Tax Not Allowed – Court Clarifies”**

The Lahore High Court has reaffirmed that agricultural income falls strictly under provincial jurisdiction and cannot be taxed by federal authorities. fileciteturn0file0  

This is an important clarification, especially in cases where the tax department attempts to reclassify agricultural income as “income from other sources” due to non-payment or documentation issues.  

In practical terms, once a taxpayer can demonstrate payment (or liability) of provincial agricultural tax, **the federal authorities cannot impose income tax on the same income**. However, where proper evidence is not maintained, the department may still attempt to tax it as unexplained income—so documentation remains critical.

---

### **4. “Crackdown on Over-Invoicing – Government Takes Strict Action”**

The government has directed immediate legal action against individuals involved in over-invoicing in imports and exports. fileciteturn0file0  

Over-invoicing has historically been used to shift funds abroad or manipulate tax liabilities. The introduction of systems like centralized price verification and increased coordination with agencies such as FIA and FMU shows a clear move towards **data-driven enforcement**.  

For businesses, this means heightened scrutiny on import/export values, and any mismatch with international benchmarks can trigger audits or investigations. Going forward, **documentation, pricing justification, and audit trails will be key to avoiding exposure**.

---

### **5. “Tax Relief on Essential Women’s Products – A Step Toward Inclusion”**

A proposal in Balochistan aims to reduce or eliminate taxes on menstrual health products to make them more affordable. fileciteturn0file0  

While this may appear as a social initiative, it reflects an important shift in tax policy—moving from pure revenue generation to **targeted relief for essential goods**.  

If implemented, such measures could set a precedent for similar exemptions or reduced tax rates on essential items across provinces, reinforcing the concept that taxation policy should also support **social equity and public welfare**.

---

### **6. “New Trade Corridor Through Iran – Big Opportunity for Exporters”**

Pakistan has operationalized a new transit trade corridor through Iran, connecting to Central Asia. fileciteturn0file0  

From a business perspective, this is a significant development. Reduced transit time and logistics costs can directly improve export competitiveness. For exporters, especially in textiles and agriculture, this opens access to new markets with potentially better margins.  

However, it also means that businesses must ensure **compliance with international trade documentation, customs valuation, and tax reporting**, as cross-border transactions will come under greater regulatory oversight.

---

**Subject:** SRB Tribunal Appeal – Reverse Charge Mechanism | Hearing Update & Way Forward  

Dear [Client Name],  

I hope you are doing well.  

As you are aware, your appeal before the Sindh Revenue Board (SRB) Tribunal relating to the Reverse Charge Mechanism was fixed for hearing yesterday. During the course of the hearing, we duly presented and elaborated our arguments before the Honorable Members. However, certain new perspectives were also introduced from the other side during the proceedings, which led to a broader discussion on the matter.  

In this context, it is pertinent to highlight that a recent judgment of the entity["organization","Sindh High Court","Pakistan High Court"] has declared the application of the reverse charge mechanism as ultra vires, thereby materially changing the legal landscape surrounding this issue.  

From your case perspective, it is important to note that the tax under reverse charge had already been deposited with SRB, and the corresponding input tax adjustment was duly claimed in the Annexure-F of your sales tax return. This adjustment, being a significant component of your case, has already been examined and accepted at the departmental level, and the same stands validated through the assessment proceedings in your favor.  

Accordingly, from a practical standpoint, the matter has already reached a stage where both the tax payment and its adjustment have been effectively settled and recognized. If the appeal is pursued further, it may lead to a situation where payments may need to be reversed or re-routed between tax authorities, potentially resulting in refund claims in one forum and tax payments in another. This would unnecessarily complicate the tax position, particularly in terms of cash flow management and procedural compliance (i.e., dealing with refund processes with SRB while corresponding liabilities may arise elsewhere).  

During the hearing, the Honorable Bench informally indicated that the matter may either be withdrawn or otherwise decided on merits. While we have already requested the Bench to proceed with a decision, the next hearing is tentatively expected to be scheduled in the last week of April (around 27th April 2026).  

In light of the above, and considering both the factual and legal position of your case—where the key adjustments have already been secured and validated—it appears that there is limited practical benefit in continuing the appeal. On the contrary, any adverse or even favorable outcome at this stage may lead to avoidable complications in implementation.  

We would therefore request you to kindly review the above position and share your considered view on whether to proceed with the appeal or opt for withdrawal, keeping in mind the overall tax efficiency and administrative implications.  

We remain available to discuss this in further detail, if required.  

Warm regards,  
[Your Name]

Therefore, the essential ingredient for imposition of penalty—i.e., deliberate default—is clearly absent.

The proceedings initiated through the instant show cause notice may kindly be dropped, as the taxpayer has neither committed any willful default nor violated the law in substance; and  
The extension already requested may kindly be granted to enable completion of integration in a technically sound and compliant manner.

The taxpayer remains fully committed to complying with all statutory requirements and assures your good office that integration will be completed at the earliest possible time. Any further developments in this regard will be promptly communicated.

### **1. Tax Disputes Should Not Take Years — Supreme Court Pushes for Faster Resolution**

The Chief Justice of Pakistan has emphasized that efficient and timely resolution of tax disputes is essential for building public trust and ensuring a predictable legal environment. fileciteturn0file0  

In practical terms, this is a significant development for businesses facing prolonged litigation. Delays caused by repetitive appeals and weak case management have long been a concern. The judiciary is now focusing on reducing unnecessary litigation and improving coordination between institutions.  

From a professional standpoint, this highlights the importance of **strong documentation, well-prepared submissions, and proactive dispute management**. Businesses that address issues early and strategically will be better positioned to avoid long-standing tax disputes.

---

### **2. Big Relief for Taxpayers? ATIR Declares Orders by Junior Officers Invalid**

In a landmark judgment, the Appellate Tribunal Inland Revenue (ATIR) has clarified that only the Commissioner Inland Revenue or Commissioner (Appeals) can pass appeal effect orders under Section 11B of the Sales Tax Act. fileciteturn0file0  

This has far-reaching implications. In many cases, such orders are issued by subordinate officers. The Tribunal has now held that such actions are **without jurisdiction and legally void**.  

For taxpayers, this creates a strong legal ground to challenge such orders. Practically, it reinforces the need to **examine not just the tax demand but also the legal authority of the officer issuing the order**.

---

### **3. FBR Moves Towards Data-Driven Tax Enforcement — Are You Prepared?**

FBR has constituted a technical committee to strengthen its Compliance Risk Management (CRM) system, aiming to identify high-risk taxpayers through advanced data analytics. fileciteturn0file0  

This marks a shift from traditional audit selection to a **data-driven enforcement model**, where discrepancies across returns, banking data, and third-party information can trigger scrutiny.  

For businesses, this means compliance must go beyond basic filing. Even minor mismatches—such as inconsistencies between sales tax and income tax declarations—can result in automated risk flags.  

The key takeaway is clear: **proper reconciliation, consistency in reporting, and robust documentation are now essential**.

---

### **4. Super Tax Controversy Deepens — Can FBR Retain Excess Tax?**

The controversy surrounding super tax under Section 4C continues to evolve, with recent judicial developments raising serious concerns regarding taxpayers’ rights. fileciteturn0file0  

While courts have treated super tax as a separate levy, an important issue remains unresolved: the treatment of **excess tax paid under protest**.  

The law clearly provides that excess tax must be **refunded or adjusted**. However, recent interpretations have overlooked these provisions, creating uncertainty for taxpayers.  

From an advisory perspective, this is critical. Many corporates have made payments under protest, and the ultimate relief may depend on higher judicial forums. Proper documentation and strategic handling of such cases will be essential.

---

### **5. Mobile Phones in Pakistan: Up to 55% Tax — Relief Still Uncertain**

Taxes on imported mobile phones in Pakistan can reach up to 55% of their value, particularly for high-end devices. fileciteturn0file0  

Although proposals have been discussed to rationalize these taxes in the upcoming budget, authorities have indicated limited room for reduction due to revenue constraints.  

For consumers, this explains the high prices. For businesses, especially importers and distributors, it underscores the need for careful pricing strategies and compliance with tax regulations.  

At the same time, lower tax rates on locally manufactured phones indicate a clear policy direction towards **supporting domestic industry**.

---

### **6. FBR Tightens Accountability — ‘Living Beyond Means’ Cases Lead to Forced Retirement**

FBR has taken strict disciplinary action against customs officials found to have assets beyond their declared income, resulting in compulsory retirement. fileciteturn0file0  

This reflects an increased focus on **financial transparency and accountability**, supported by stronger enforcement mechanisms.  

For taxpayers, this carries an important message. Authorities are increasingly using data integration to compare declared income with assets. Any unexplained difference can lead to serious consequences.  

A common practical scenario includes property purchases or investments without declared income support—such cases are now more likely to be scrutinized.

---

Dear Najeeb,

With reference to the reconciliation of PIFU Technical Services, we would like to clarify that the subject notice contains a fundamental error at the outset. The officer, without examining the underlying factual details, has deducted the entire expense figure as recorded in our accounts, which has consequently resulted in an inflated shortfall. However, this approach is not in line with the actual mechanics of the reconciliation.

In substance, the correct treatment should have been to deduct only the value of services declared as FTS during the period January 2017 to December 2017, on which sales tax had already been charged and duly reported. The aggregated taxable value for this period was already available, and therefore, only the corresponding declared component should have been adjusted to arrive at the true taxable value of the remaining services. The adjustment made by the officer, based on the P&L expense figure (approximately PKR 600 million), appears to be based on an incorrect presumption and does not reflect the actual tax position.

Given that this was essentially a mathematical correction, we believe that a detailed reconciliation was not warranted at the outset, and the direction taken during the proceedings to provide reconciliation was not aligned with the core issue. The matter could have been resolved by simply aligning the declared FTS values for the relevant period.

For completeness, we would also like to highlight that the portion relating to the last quarter (i.e., December 2017) would naturally not reconcile within the same period due to accrual-based reporting, and the corresponding sales tax liability was discharged in the subsequent period. A review of the January 2018 return would have readily reconciled this difference.

Nevertheless, for your ease, we have now prepared and enclosed a detailed reconciliation along with the necessary break-up. We are also attaching the January 2018 return for your reference, wherein the relevant declarations can be verified on Page 10, Serial Nos. 260 to 263. Based on this, the figures largely reconcile with the amounts reflected in the P&L for the period January to December 2017, with a minor variance (approximately PKR 9 million), which may be attributable to exchange differences or similar adjustments.

We would also request that, going forward, a preliminary review of available records—particularly subsequent period returns—may be undertaken, as such straightforward reconciliations can often be identified at that stage.

With respect to the invoice-wise listing, we are in the process of compiling the complete details. We will endeavor to share the same with you today; however, at the latest, this will be provided by Sunday. The listing will cover the entire revenue base, including both imports and exports. As discussed earlier, once a reasonable sample is identified, we will also arrange to provide the corresponding invoices for verification.

Please feel free to reach out should you require any further clarification.

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]

It is a settled principle, as consistently upheld by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan, that the characterization of income must be determined with reference to its real source, surrounding circumstances, and nexus with the taxpayer’s business. In the case of *Fauji Foundation*, the Hon’ble Court recognized that income arising from activities aligned with the core business objectives, including returns on funds deployed within the business structure, constitutes business income and cannot be treated as a separate or independent stream merely due to its form. The statutory language of section 39(1) itself makes it clear that it covers income “other than” that chargeable under any other provision of the Ordinance. Accordingly, where income is properly classifiable under section 18 as business income, it cannot be simultaneously or alternatively brought to tax under section 39. ### **REASONS FOR GRANT OF STAY**

The Appellant respectfully submits that the impugned demand has arisen due to fundamental mischaracterization of income and disregard of settled legal principles, thereby giving rise to a strong prima facie case in favour of the Appellant. ---

### **1. Profit on Debt – Integral to Business Operations, Not Income from Other Sources**

The principal issue relates to the treatment of profit on debt, which has been incorrectly classified under section 39 as “Income from Other Sources.” The Appellant’s case is that such income arises from mandatory placement of funds in designated security accounts under binding project financing arrangements, forming an inseparable part of its LNG terminal business. The earning of such profit is not the result of any independent or discretionary investment activity, but is an automatic consequence of lender-imposed financing covenants.

The department’s approach of isolating such income is contrary to settled law that the character of income must be determined based on its real source and nexus with business operations. In this regard, reliance is placed on judicial precedents including **Commissioner of Income Tax v. Pioneer Cement (2005 PTD 2086)**, wherein it has been held that interest earned on funds having direct nexus with business and corresponding borrowings cannot be treated in isolation, and must be assessed in the correct commercial context. Further, in **AES Lalpir (Pvt.) Ltd. (ITA Nos. 624–627/LB/2008)** and **Nishat Power Limited (ITA Nos. 1521 & 1522/LB/2011)**, the Hon’ble Tribunal has held that where deposits are maintained under financing requirements, the resultant income is intrinsically linked with business operations and the related finance cost is allowable. fileciteturn0file0  

Without prejudice, even if such income is treated under section 39, the corresponding finance cost incurred on the same borrowed funds is mandatorily allowable under section 40. This principle stands settled through consistent judicial pronouncements, including **Lalpir Power (2014 PTD 842)** and **Kohinoor Energy Limited (2021 SLD 908)**, where it has been held that taxation must be on net income after allowing expenditure directly incurred in earning such income. The impugned order, by taxing gross receipts without allowing corresponding costs, is therefore contrary to both the statutory scheme and binding precedent. fileciteturn0file0  

---

### **2. Other Receivables – Integral Accretion to Business Receipts**

The second issue pertains to the treatment of certain receivables (including amounts arising under the LNG Services Agreement) which have been separately taxed as “other income.” The department has failed to appreciate that such receipts are not independent income streams but represent accretions to amounts arising under the same underlying business contract.

The law on this point is well-settled. The Hon’ble Appellate Tribunal in **Lalpir Power Limited (ITA No. 894/LB/2012 dated October 24, 2012)** and subsequently in **Hub Power Company Limited (ITA No. 917/IB/2012 dated February 26, 2013)** has categorically held that where receipts arise under the same contract, any accretion thereto retains the same character as the principal receipt and cannot be artificially segregated for separate taxation. This principle has further been affirmed in **Engro Powergen Qadirpur Limited (ITA No. 905/KB/2013 and ITA No. 489/KB/2015)**, where it was held that all receipts under a single contractual framework partake the same nature for tax purposes. fileciteturn0file1  

In the present case, the receivables in question arise directly from the LNG Services Agreement and are intrinsically linked to the Appellant’s core business of terminal operations. The impugned treatment, by isolating and taxing these amounts separately, disregards the settled legal position and results in distortion of the true nature of business income.

---

### **Conclusion – Prima Facie Case, Irreparable Loss & Balance of Convenience**

In view of the above, it is respectfully submitted that the Appellant has a strong prima facie case supported by binding judicial precedents and consistent legal principles. The issues involved are substantial and arguable, and the impugned demand is prima facie unsustainable.

Recovery at this stage would cause irreparable financial prejudice and disrupt the Appellant’s operations, whereas no prejudice would be caused to the revenue if recovery is stayed, as the Appellant is a compliant taxpayer with sound financial standing.

It is therefore respectfully prayed that this Hon’ble Tribunal may be pleased to grant stay against recovery of the impugned demand till final disposal of the appeal.

This principle has been consistently upheld in various judicial pronouncements, where courts have emphasized that taxation must follow the concept of real income rather than notional adjustments.

From a practical standpoint:

- Where borrowings are denominated in foreign currency, the liability **fluctuates with exchange rates**.
- Under IFRS (IAS 21), such revaluation is **compulsory**, not discretionary.
- Courts in Pakistan have consistently held that:
  - Exchange loss on foreign currency liabilities is **revenue in nature** if related to business operations.
  - Even if unrealized, it represents a **real diminution in liability value**, not a fictitious entry.

**Strong position to take:**
This is not a “notional loss” but a **recognized business expense arising from an existing enforceable liability**, hence outside the scope of section 34(3).

You may reinforce this with case law (e.g., principles laid down in exchange fluctuation cases such as *Woodward Governor (India)*—though Indian, often relied upon locally—and local tribunal precedents).

---

### **1. “Rs. 5.4 Trillion Stuck in Tax Litigation – Why It Matters to You”**

Pakistan’s tax system is currently burdened with over **Rs. 5.4 trillion locked in litigation**, with thousands of cases pending at tribunal and court levels. fileciteturn0file0  

This is not just a government issue—it directly affects businesses and taxpayers. When disputes remain unresolved for years, companies face **cash flow pressure, uncertainty in tax positions, and difficulty in long-term planning**. In many cases, even after taxpayers win at one level, the matter continues through appeals, increasing legal costs and delaying final resolution.

From a practical standpoint, this reflects a system where **litigation has become routine rather than exceptional**. Instead of resolving issues at the assessment stage, matters are pushed forward, often unnecessarily.

For businesses, the key takeaway is to **maintain strong documentation and adopt defensible tax positions**, because disputes today are not just about law—they are about endurance over time.

---

### **2. “IT Export Income: Relief Confirmed, But Documentation is Everything”**

The recent ATIR ruling reinforces that **foreign remittances from IT and software exports are exempt from tax**, provided they fall under the relevant exemption provisions. fileciteturn0file0  

However, what is important in this case is not just the relief—but the **reason the dispute arose**. The tax authorities treated legitimate export income as unexplained under Section 111, primarily due to lack of proper linkage or clarity in documentation.

This is a very common issue in practice. Many freelancers and IT exporters receive foreign remittances but fail to maintain:
- Proper bank remittance evidence  
- Export registration or certification  
- Clear reconciliation with declared income  

The Tribunal’s decision shows that the law supports taxpayers—but **only when facts are properly demonstrated**.

In real terms, exemption is not automatic. It is **compliance-driven**, and documentation is your strongest defence.

---

### **3. “110% Increase in Audit Recoveries – What It Means for Taxpayers”**

FBR has reported a significant **110% increase in audit-based recoveries**, reaching Rs. 267 billion in FY 2024–25. fileciteturn0file0  

On paper, this reflects improved enforcement and better audit selection. However, from a professional standpoint, it also indicates that the tax department is increasingly relying on **data analytics and risk profiling** to identify taxpayers for audit.

In practical terms, this means:
- Random audits are reducing  
- Targeted audits based on data mismatches are increasing  

For example, differences between:
- Sales tax returns and income tax returns  
- Bank transactions and declared turnover  
- Withholding tax statements and income declared  

can easily trigger audit proceedings.

The message for taxpayers is clear: **consistency across all filings is no longer optional**. Even minor mismatches can lead to detailed scrutiny and additional tax exposure.

---

### **4. “Record Tax Filing – But Compliance Still Has a Long Way to Go”**

Pakistan has achieved record tax payments of **Rs. 222 billion with return filings**, showing improved compliance trends. fileciteturn0file0  

While this appears encouraging, a deeper look reveals that payments with returns still form only about **4% of total tax collection**. This means the system still depends heavily on **withholding taxes and indirect taxation**.

From a practical advisory perspective, this indicates two realities:
- More people are entering the tax system  
- But true voluntary compliance is still evolving  

For individuals and businesses, being a filer now impacts:
- Banking transactions  
- Property purchases  
- Business credibility  

So, compliance is no longer just about avoiding penalties—it is about **remaining economically active without restrictions**.

---

### **5. “Reduction in FBR Arrest Powers – A Shift Towards Trust-Based Taxation”**

The recent reforms reducing the **arrest powers of FBR officials** mark an important shift in Pakistan’s tax environment. fileciteturn0file0  

Historically, such powers created fear among businesses, particularly SMEs and traders, where enforcement sometimes appeared excessive or inconsistent.

By limiting these powers, the government is trying to create a system based more on:
- **Predictability**
- **Transparency**
- **Taxpayer confidence**

However, it is important to understand that this does not reduce tax liability or compliance requirements. Instead, it ensures that enforcement is carried out in a more structured and legally balanced manner.

For businesses, this is a positive signal—but it also means that **compliance will increasingly be monitored through data and systems rather than physical enforcement**.

---

### **6. “Default Surcharge on Super Tax – A Critical Legal Debate”**

The issue of **default surcharge on super tax** has become a major concern for the corporate sector. fileciteturn0file0  

The fundamental principle is that default surcharge under Section 205 applies only when there is a **clear and enforceable tax liability**. However, in many cases, super tax liability was under litigation and subject to court orders.

In such situations:
- The tax liability is considered **suspended or uncertain**  
- Therefore, the condition of “failure to pay” does not exist  

This position is well supported by legal principles and court precedents.

From a practical standpoint, many companies paid super tax later after clarity emerged. Imposing surcharge retrospectively in such cases raises serious legal concerns.

For taxpayers facing such notices, this is not just a compliance issue—it is a **strong litigation point with reasonable chances of relief**.

---

### **7. “Rs. 520 Million Customs Fraud – What It Reveals About the System”**

The exposure of a **Rs. 520 million customs fraud** has highlighted serious weaknesses in the system, particularly in the newly introduced faceless assessment mechanism. fileciteturn0file0

- Lack of effective controls  
- Weak enforcement at key stages  
- Possible internal collusion  

For legitimate businesses, such incidents often lead to **stricter regulations and increased scrutiny**, even for compliant taxpayers.

In practical terms, importers should now expect:
- More detailed examination of consignments  
- Greater reliance on risk-based profiling  
- Increased documentation requirements  

This is a classic situation where **system failures result in tighter controls for everyone**.

parts: At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that at Issue No. 2 of the show cause notice, your good office has expressly acknowledged that our client has duly offered exchange gain on lease receivables amounting to Rs. 4,761,704,000/- to tax. Notwithstanding this clear admission, the notice proceeds to single out only the corresponding unrealized exchange loss of Rs. 4,039,055,000/- for disallowance under section 34(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. With due respect, such an approach reflects a selective and one-sided appreciation of the underlying facts, as both the exchange gain and exchange loss emanate from the same pool of foreign currency denominated assets and are accounted for in accordance with consistent and recognized accounting principles. Isolating the loss component while accepting the gain effectively amounts to cherry-picking of only the adverse element, which distorts the true and fair view of income already offered to tax by our client in the form of net exchange gain.

Please read below the issue raised in the assessment notice. Please prepare a combined introduction paragraph: 

As per note.28 to the financial statement, you have claimed unrealized exchange loss on revaluation of borrowings at Rs.261,130,000/- and claimed as admissible deduction. Said deduction is inadmissible in terms of section 34(3) of the Ordinance being notional in nature. You are therefore show cause as to why claim of unrealized exchange loss may not be disallowed and added back to your total 
income for the year under consideration in terms of section 34(3) of the Ordinance.


As per note-27 to the audited financial statements, you have declared exchange gain on lease receivables at Rs.4,761,704,000/-; however, further perusal of said note it is noted that said gain has been adjusted unrealized exchange loss of Rs.4,039,055,000/- net gain has been declared at Rs. 45,993,000/-. Deduction claimed in respect of unrealized exchange loss is required to be disallowed 
being notional in nature in terms of section 34(3) of the Ordinance. Please explain as to why not the said claim of unrealized losses aggregating to Rs.4,039,055,000/- may be disallowed as deduction and added to your income under section 34(3) of the ITO, 2001.

Please read the below and prepare conclusion paragraph: 

2.1	Through the subject notice, your good office has observed that our client has claimed unrealized exchange loss on revaluation of borrowings amounting to Rs 261,130,000 as disclosed in note No. 28 to the financial statements, and has treated the same as an admissible deduction. Further, with reference to note No. 27 of the audited financial statements, it has been noted that exchange gain on lease receivables amounting to Rs 4,761,704,000 has been reported, against which an unrealized exchange loss of Rs 4,039,055,000 has been adjusted, resulting in a net gain of Rs 45,993,000. 

2.2	It has been contended in the notice that the aforesaid unrealized exchange losses are notional in nature and, therefore, inadmissible under section 34(3) of the Ordinance. Accordingly, our client has been called upon to justify the allowability of such losses and to explain as to why the aggregate unrealized exchange losses should not be disallowed and added back to the total income for the year under consideration.

2.3	At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that at issue No. 2 of the subject notice, your good office has expressly acknowledged that our client has duly offered unrealized exchange gain on lease receivables amounting to 
Rs 4,761,704,000 to tax. Notwithstanding this clear admission, the notice proceeds to single out only the corresponding unrealized exchange loss of Rs 4,039,055,000 for disallowance under section 34(3) of the Ordinance. 

2.4	With due respect, such an approach reflects a selective and one-sided appreciation of the underlying facts, as both the exchange gain and exchange loss emanate from the same pool of foreign currency denominated assets and are accounted for in accordance with consistent and recognized accounting principles. Isolating the loss component while accepting the gain effectively amounts to cherry-picking of only the adverse element, which distorts the true and fair view of income already offered to tax by our client in the form of net exchange gain.

2.5	It is pertinent to mention here that books of account of our client are maintained under the mercantile / accrual system of accounting and accordingly the claim these expenses are allowable to our client on accrual basis following the decisions of superior courts. It is respectfully submitted that the issue raised in the subject notice is no longer open to debate and stands conclusively settled in favour of the taxpayer by the superior courts. In this regard, we would draw your kind attention to the judgment of the Hon’ble Sindh High Court reported as 2022 PTD 1535, wherein the Hon’ble Court has affirmed the action of the learned ATIR in allowing exchange difference on accrual basis. 

2.6	The Hon’ble Court has unequivocally held that exchange differences arising on foreign currency liabilities constitute an ascertained liability and are allowable under the mercantile system of accounting. It has further been observed that such exchange fluctuation, though not settled in cash terms at the reporting date, represents a real and determinable liability, duly recognized in accordance with the accounting system regularly employed, and therefore qualifies as a lawful deduction under Sections 32 and 34 of the Ordinance. For the sake of brevity, the relevant operative paragraph is reproduced below:

“12. In the instant matter it has not been disputed that certain amount was payable by the respondent to its foreign company, which, in our view, has to be considered as an ascertained liability and allowance of the same has to be made on accrual basis, as per the mercantile system of accounting, and the extra amount payable at the time of actual payments due to the devaluation of the rupee, has to be taken care of in the accounts as an ascertained liability of the respondent, as per the accounting system employed, which has to be considered as a lawful deduction in the hands of the respondent. The decisions relied upon by the learned counsel for the respondents also speaks of the situation that if the amount is accrued and ascertained, but actual payment is made afterwards, the same would be an allowable expenditure, as per the system of accounting maintained by the said person. Hence the entries made in the books of accounts, as per the accounting method followed by the respondent, being mercantile are to be considered as valid entries for the purposes of allowing the said exchange loss.

13. We, therefore, are of the view that the order of CIRA and ATIR do not suffer from any legal infirmity and have been passed in conformity with the provisions of Sections 32 read with Section 34 of the Ordinance. We, therefore, answer the question No.2 in affirmative i.e. in favour of the respondent and against the applicant. The instant ITRA stands disposed of in the above terms.
									    (emphasis is our)


2.7	It is further submitted that the aforesaid judgment has attained finality upon dismissal of the departmental appeal by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan, which declined leave to appeal, thereby affirming the concurrent findings of the appellate authorities and the High Court. Copies of the said judgments of the Hon’ble Sindh High Court and the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan are enclosed herewith as Annexure ‘A’ and Annexure ‘B’, respectively, for your ready reference. For the sake of ready reference, the relevant operative paragraph is reproduced below:

“The matter agitated before us involves technicalities and intricacies of accounting, which had been attended to in the above mentioned orders. which this Court is not inclined to reverse, particularly in view of the said three concurrent decisions. Therefore, leave to appeal is declined and, consequently, this petition is dismissed.”
										     (emphasis is our)

2.8	In view of this settled and binding legal position, the contention advanced in the notice that unrealized exchange loss is merely notional and inadmissible under section 34(3) is legally untenable and contrary to the law laid down by the superior courts.

2.9	Without prejudice to the above, section 32 read with section 34(3) of the Ordinance lays down the basis of amounts to be treated as payable by a taxpayer i.e. when all the events that determine the liability have occurred and the amount of the liability can be ascertained with reasonable accuracy. Under the accrual method, ‘fixing’ and ‘determination of amount’ of the liability with reasonable accuracy is made once the events determining the liability have occurred. The amounts are recorded in the books when liability / asset is ascertained. The basis of assertion that the asset / liability is being considered as ‘notional gain/ loss’ is totally unwarranted. This premise represents an incorrect understanding of the nature of transaction and is unwarranted on facts and circumstances of the case. 

2.10	For accounting purposes, the gain / loss is ‘unrealized’ as the same is to be realized on the date of payment / receipt but since the ‘event’ determining the liability / asset has occurred, the same is to be accounted for and if in this process, the asset / liability is in foreign currency the same is to be recorded as required under section 71 of the Ordinance.

2.11	If the provisions of section 71 of the Ordinance require that amount is to be converted into Rupees in a certain manner then all effects, i.e. the debit (including unrealized loss) or credit (including unrealized gain) to the profit and loss account as required to apply the law in the manner laid down are consequential and do not warrant disallowance merely on the basis that these are notional. Any such proposition renders the said provision of the law as redundant. Section 71 of the Ordinance states that:

“71. Currency conversion. — (1) Every amount taken into account under this Ordinance shall be in Rupees.

(2) Where an amount is in a currency other than rupees, the amount shall be converted to the Rupee at the State Bank of Pakistan rate applying between the foreign currency and the Rupee on the date the amount is taken into account for the purposes of this Ordinance.”


2.12	We reiterate that since the exchange loss booked in the audited financial statements is in accordance with the mercantile / accrual basis under section 32(2) read with section 34(3) of the Ordinance, the same is deductible for tax purposes. Thus, the issue of allowance or taxation on the basis of “realization” does not arise under any of the provisions of the Ordinance.

2.13	This represents a settled issue at higher appellate forums and there are several decisions of Tribunal wherein the issue of allowability of unrealized exchange loss has been allowed in favour of taxpayers as follows:

ITA NO. 206/KB/2016 DATED 14.12.2021 [PHILLIP MORRIS (PAKISTAN) LIMITED]

The extract of page 17 of the order is reproduced as under:

“We have considered the arguments of the AR and DR and also perused the evidence and case laws relied upon during the course of hearing. Since the issue of the allowability of unrealized exchange loss or taxability of unrealized exchange gain is now catered in the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 and there is a specific section 71 which has now resolved this issue. Now the appellant would be allowed deduction of unrealized exchange loss and any unrealized exchange gain will be tax. This issue has also been decided by tribunal in a number of decisions as quoted supra. We respectfully follow the same. However, tax officer is directed to allow the claim of unrealized exchange loss to the appellant after verifying whether the appellant has offered to tax unrealized exchange gains in subsequent years.”  (emphasis is ours)


ITA NO. 1279/KB/2017 DATED 30.11.2020 [PARAZELSUS PAKISTAN (PVT) LTD]

The extract of page 10 & 11 of the order is reproduced as under:

“22. The learned DR on the matter of exchange loss, heavily placed reliance on the decision of CIRA wherever the CIRA has upheld the disallowance of exchange loss on the ground that it is merely un-realized loss and that section 71 do no entitle taxpayer to claim the expenditure under section 34 of the Ordinance.

23. On merit, we also agree with the arguments of AR that exchange loss arising on un-paid foreign currency liability, accrued as per exchange rate prevailing year-end rate, is an ascertained liability, and is an allowable deduction under section 32 read with section 34(3) of the Ordinance. This Tribunal has already adjudicated the issue in favour of taxpayer in the case of M/s. Qasim International Container Terminal bearing ITA No. 151/KB/2014 (Tax year 2004). Hence, in terms of these statutory provisions followed in number of decisions of ATIR referred supra, we direct to delete the disallowance of exchange loss of Rs 1,208,830.”


ITA 988/KB/2013 DATED 05.07.2017 [QASIM INTERNATIONAL CONTAINER TERMINAL PAKISTAN LIMITED]

The extract of page 8 of the order is reproduced below:

“17. ……… However, without going into detail, the AR referred to ATIR’s decision in appellant’s own case  in ITA No. 20/KB of 2014 dated December 19, 2016 and ITA No. 987/KB of 2013 dated April 26, 2017 wherein in para 29 of ITA No. 20/KB of 2014 for tax year 2008 it is held that:

“On merit, we also agree with arguments of AR that exchange loss rising on un-paid foreign currency liability, accrued as per exchange rate prevailing at year-end rate, is in ascertained liability, and is an allowable deduction under section 32 read with section 34(3) of the Ordinance. Hence, in terms of these statutory provisions followed in number of decisions of ATIR referred supra, and in some decisions by this bench, we direct to delete disallowance of exchange loss of Rs. 958,000.”

18. Since the above matter has already been decided in appellant's own case in prior years hence following the same, we allow the appeal of the appellant and direct to delete the disallowance of Rs. 1.709(M).”


ITA Nos. 577/KB/2016, 1474/KB/2015, etc. dated 08.09.2021  [QASIM INTERNATIONAL CONTAINER TERMINAL LIMITED]

The extract of page 10 & 11 of the order is reproduced below:

“15. 6th issue relating to disallowing unrealized exchange loss is concerned, we find that the learned CIR(A) has confirmed the ACIR order wherein disallowing the unrealized exchange loss. Before us learn the learned AR has submitted copies of orders of this tribunal in taxpayer owned cases passed in ITA Nos. 987/KB/2013 dated 26-4-2017, ITA No. 988/KB/2013 dated 5-7-2017 and ITA No. 20/KB/2014 dated 19-12-2016, wherein the issue in hand has decided in favour of the taxpayer. After perusal of record reveals that issue in hand has already been decided by this Tribunal in favor of taxpayer in the above cited judgments. We respectfully follow judgment of this tribunal cited supra, the impugned order passed by the learned CRA on this issue is vacated and to allow the appeal of the taxpayer. 

16. Hence, the appeal filed by the taxpayer on this show is allowed all appeals filed by the taxpayer are decided in the manner as indicated.”  


ITA 1480 & 1481 / KB / 2019 DATED 26.02.2020 [ENGRO FERTILIZERS LIMITED]

The extract of page 41 & 42 of the order is reproduced as under:

80. We have heard the arguments advanced by both the parties and have pursued the available record of the case as well as the decisions of appellate authorities including this bench relied on by the learned AR. While making the addition the main contention of the taxation officer is that the liability is not ascertained and unrealised loss is not claimable under section 32 of read with section 34(3) of the Ordinance. 

81. The learned AR on other hand argued before us that the exchange loss is in relation to the issue foreign loans which fact is not disputed by the learned DR. This bench of the tribunal has already adjudicated in the context of the application of the provisions of section 71 read with sections 32 and 34(3) of the Ordinance the issue of unrealised exchange laws on loans while deciding the appeals in the case of other taxpayers in ITA Nos. 151 to 155/KB/2012 dated 6.05.2019 as quoted below:

“24. The main contention of the officer is again that the liability is not ascertained and unrealised loss is not claimable under section 32 read with section 34(3) of the Ordinance. The facts of the matter are that this bench of the Tribunal has already adjudicated in the taxpayers’ own case in relation to the loan liability which is confirmed, proper and was duly registered with the State Bank of Pakistan. In our view there is clarity on ‘due date’ and the amount of payment which ‘is in US$’ and also has been so discharged and it is also required to be accounted for by the company under section 32(2) of the Ordinance on accrual basis consistently followed at year end being determined at each date with reasonable accuracy and exchange loss arising on un-paid foreign currency liability which was accrued as per exchange rate prevailing at year-end rate is an ascertained liability and is an allowable deduction under section 32 read with section 34(3) of the ordinance. This principle of law on given facts has already been decided by this Bench in the company's own case through combined appellate order in ITA No.s 694/KB/2013, 695/KB/2013, 168/KB/2014 and 235/KB/2014 dated March 8, 2018 for tax years 2010 to 2-12. In light of said principal we direct to delete the disallowance of exchange loss.”

82. Accordingly, following our earlier judgments and reasons contained therein in detail, we hereby order to delete the disallowance of exchange loss made under section 34(3) of the ordinance.


ITA NO. 967/KB/2018 DATED 29.01.2020 [BAKRI ENERGY PVT LTD]

The extract of page 8 & 9 of the order is reproduced as under:

“17. In furtherance to the above submissions, the AR argued that the admissibility of exchange loss has already been decided by the Tribunal in appellant’s own case for tax year 2012 in ITA No. 197/KB/2014 dated June 2, 2016 as under:

The Learned AR of the taxpayer further argued that the said exchange loss of Rs 50.215(M) is admittedly, on Foreign Currency Loans obtained by the taxpayer company and also repayable in Foreign Currency, as per agreement with the Foreign lender. The agreement is also registered with the State Bank of Pakistan and therefore, at the balance sheet date of 30th June, 2012, such loan was converted at SBP rates of foreign currency and exchange loss computed/ resulted therefore is admittedly, capitalized to such loan, as full working of exchange loss submitted with the assessing officer and also with CIR(A) and as evidenced by the audited financial statement. Therefore, the claim of such exchange loss is not notional loss but is construed as payment as verified by the CIR(A) from the facts and evidences and therefore, it is correctly directed by CIR(A) to allow the same as admissible.

18. In view of the above referred order of the Tribunal in appellant’s own case as well as certain other decisions of the Hon’ble High Court and Tribunal, the AR prayed that the appellant’s claim for admissibility of exchange loss be allowed.”


ITA No. 391/KB/2001-2002 & ITA No. 392/ KB/ 2001-2002 DATED 23.02.2011

The extract of page 4 of the order is reproduced as under:

“17.	We have considered the contentions of the learned AR and DR. It would be worth mentioning that the allowability of unrealized exchange loss or taxability of unrealized exchange gain is catered in the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. There is a specific section 71 which has now resolved this issue. Now the appellant would be allowed deduction of unrealized exchange loss and any unrealized exchange gain will be tax. However, the year of the appellant which is before us is not governed by the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 but unfortunately for the appellant is governed by the Income Tax Ordinance, 1979. The old Ordinance does not have a specific provision for such a situation. Therefore, in the absence of section similar to section 71 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001, the unrealized exchange loss is not an allowable deduction.” (emphasis is ours)

18. The plea of the AR that the unrealized loss became realized subsequent to the year end; and it should then be allowed, is justified. The assessing officer is directed to allow the claim if payment of foreign currency liability had been made subsequently. The claim is to be allowed in the years of actual payment after necessary verification that actual payment had occurred.” 


(2011) 103 TAX 14 DATED 29.09.2010 [FAUJI FERTILIZER COMPANY LIMITED]

The extract of page 26 & 27 of the order is reproduced as under:
“The Company has contested the order of the CIR(A) whereby he has upheld the order of the Additional Commissioner disallowing the exchange loss of 
Rs. 35,556,823 on the ground that the same is notional loss which cannot be claimed as deduction. On the other hand the DR has supported the order of CIR(A). 

Since exchange loss is admissible on realized basis and I agree on this score with CIR(A) as held by him in his appellate order. However, due to peculiar circumstances in the present case that Company has not claimed the said exchange loss in tax year, 2009 and Additional Commissioner has also not the same in subsequent tax year, we feel that if would be in the interest justice to allow the same in tax year, 2008 keeping in view the judgment of the Tribunal reported as 2008 PTD (Trib) 1040 referred by AR in his arguments. In the said judgment Tribunal has allowed exchange loss on mercantile system of accounting duly followed by the taxpayer and accepted by the Department in the past. Accordingly, company’s appeal is accepted on this issue and addition made by the Additional Commissioner is deleted and order of CIR(A) is modified against to this extent.”

It is respectfully submitted that the issue raised in the subject notice is no longer open to debate and stands conclusively settled in favour of the taxpayer by the superior courts. In this regard, reliance is placed on the judgment of the Hon’ble Sindh High Court reported as *2022 PTD 1535*, wherein it has been unequivocally held that exchange differences arising on foreign currency liabilities constitute an ascertained liability and are allowable on accrual basis under the mercantile system of accounting. The Hon’ble Court has specifically observed that such exchange fluctuation, though not settled in cash terms at the reporting date, represents a real and determinable liability, duly recognized in accordance with the accounting system regularly employed, and therefore qualifies as a lawful deduction under Sections 32 and 34 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 fileciteturn0file1L30-L36.  

It is further submitted that the aforesaid judgment has attained finality upon dismissal of the departmental appeal by the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan, which declined leave to appeal, thereby affirming the concurrent findings of the appellate authorities and the High Court fileciteturn0file0L6-L13. Copies of the said judgments of the Hon’ble Sindh High Court and the Hon’ble Supreme Court of Pakistan are enclosed herewith as *Annexure “A”* and *Annexure “B”*, respectively, for your ready reference.  

In view of this settled and binding legal position, the contention advanced in the notice that unrealized exchange loss is merely notional and inadmissible under section 34(3) is legally untenable and contrary to the law laid down by the superior courts.

**Reversal of Provision for Diesel – Allowability of Deduction**

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the observation made in the subject notice proceeds on an incorrect appreciation of both facts and the applicable legal principles. The amount of Rs. 198,432,000/- represents reversal of provision for diesel, which had earlier been recognized in the books in accordance with the applicable accounting standards under the mercantile system of accounting consistently followed by our client.

It is a settled principle that under the accrual basis of accounting, provisions are created when a liability is reasonably estimated, and subsequently reversed when the liability either does not materialize or is determined at a lower amount. Such reversal does not constitute an independent “deduction” claimed by the taxpayer; rather, it is merely an accounting adjustment impacting the net expense recognized during the year. In substance, the reversal reduces the overall expense charged to profit and loss account and, therefore, has the effect of increasing taxable income rather than reducing it.

Without prejudice, even if the contention of your good office is considered, the premise that deduction is allowable only if the provision was previously “offered to tax” is not applicable in the present case. The provision for diesel, when initially recognized, formed part of the expense base in a year where the income was exempt, and therefore no tax benefit was derived by the taxpayer. Consequently, the subsequent reversal cannot be selectively disallowed, as this would lead to an anomalous situation where expense is effectively taxed twice—once by denying the deduction in the year of reversal, despite no corresponding tax benefit having been availed earlier.

It is further submitted that the provisions of section 34(3) deal with the timing and recognition of liabilities under accrual accounting, i.e., when an amount becomes “payable.” The said provision has no application to a case of reversal of provision, which, by its very nature, reflects cessation or reduction of an earlier estimated liability and not the incurrence of a fresh liability.

In view of the above, the reversal of provision for diesel has been correctly accounted for in accordance with the mercantile system and does not give rise to any inadmissible deduction. Accordingly, the proposed disallowance is based on an erroneous understanding of both facts and law and is liable to be dropped.

Here is a refined, structured, and technically aligned response incorporating your points, removing ambiguity, and properly presenting the client’s explanation:

---

**Issue No. __: Treatment of recovery of construction cost of SSGC branch pipeline**

**6.1** Through the subject notice, your good office has observed that, as per note 23 to the audited financial statements, our client has deducted an amount of Rs 215,637,000 from the gross revenue of Rs 18,901,983,000 on account of recovery of construction cost of SSGC branch pipeline along with related interest. Accordingly, our client has been called upon to justify the said treatment and to show cause as to why the aforesaid amount should not be added back to total income.

**6.2** At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the subject observation lacks any specific legal basis, as the notice does not refer to any particular provision of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (the Ordinance) under which the proposed addition is sought to be made. In absence of identification of any charging or disallowance provision, the observation remains general in nature and effectively constitutes a **fishing inquiry**, whereby clarification has been sought without first establishing any prima facie inadmissibility.

**6.3** Without prejudice to the above, it is submitted that the amount in question has been incorrectly interpreted as a “deduction” from revenue. In substance, the treatment relates to **recovery of construction cost of SSGC branch pipeline**, which is capital in nature and does not constitute revenue of the company. Accordingly, the same has been adjusted against revenue in order to reflect the true and correct operational income, in line with applicable accounting principles.

**6.4** For clarity, it is submitted that the overall accounting impact of the said treatment is as follows:
- Out of the total amount of Rs 215,637,000, a sum of approximately Rs 171 million has been recognized under **other income**;
- The underlying infrastructure (SSGC pipeline) has been recognized as an **asset** in the books of the company;
- An amount of approximately Rs 44 million represents **amortization** charged during the year.

Thus, the **net impact on profit and loss account is approximately Rs 45 million**, which has already been duly reflected in the financial results.

**6.5** It is therefore evident that there is no suppression of income or undue reduction of taxable profits. The treatment merely reflects the correct classification between capital recovery and revenue income, along with corresponding recognition of amortization over the useful life of the asset. The accounting entries are interlinked and cannot be viewed in isolation by picking a single line item from the notes.

**6.6** It is further submitted that if the amount of Rs 215,637,000 is artificially added back to income without considering the corresponding recognition of other income and amortization, it would lead to **distortion of taxable income** and result in double counting, which is not permissible under the law.

**6.7** In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the treatment adopted by our client is in accordance with sound accounting principles and does not result in any inadmissible deduction or understatement of income. The proposed addition, being based on an incomplete appreciation of facts and without reference to any specific provision of law, is therefore unwarranted and liable to be dropped in entirety.

---

**Issue No. __: Alleged non-payment / refund claim of Super Tax under section 4C**

**8.1** Through the subject notice, your good office has observed that, as per the revised return of income, our client has incorporated payment of Super Tax under section 4C of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (the Ordinance) amounting to Rs 328,300,000, without charging the same in the computation of total income and has consequently claimed the said amount as refundable. On this basis, our client has been called upon to explain as to why the amount of Super Tax may not be charged and recovered under section 4C(4)/(5) read with section 122(5A) of the Ordinance.

**8.2** At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the treatment adopted in the revised return was based on the legal position prevailing at the relevant time, wherein the levy of Super Tax under section 4C was subject to judicial scrutiny before various High Courts. In particular, the Honourable Sindh High Court, through its judgment, had held that the imposition of Super Tax for the relevant period suffered from legal infirmities, including the issue of retrospectivity. Accordingly, the computation adopted by our client was aligned with the then prevailing judicial position.

**8.3** It is further submitted that subsequent to the above, the matter has attained finality through the judgment of the Honourable Supreme Court / Federal Constitutional Court, wherein the levy of Super Tax under section 4C has been upheld. In view of the said development, our client has duly complied with the law and has **discharged the Super Tax liability**, to the extent applicable, in accordance with the final judicial determination.

**8.4** In this regard, it is important to clarify that the amount of Rs 328,300,000 was initially reflected in the return in a protective manner, given the then prevailing uncertainty regarding enforceability of the levy. However, following the final adjudication by the Honourable Supreme Court / Federal Constitutional Court, the liability stands regularized and has been appropriately dealt with by our client. Therefore, there remains no basis for any further charge or recovery on this account.

**8.5** Without prejudice to the above, it is also submitted that any action under section 122(5A) must be based on a demonstrable error or omission in the assessment which is prejudicial to the interest of revenue. In the present case, the matter relates to a legal interpretation which was subject to judicial proceedings at the relevant time, and the treatment adopted by our client was fully supported by the prevailing legal position. Accordingly, the same cannot be characterized as an error warranting amendment under section 122(5A).

**8.6** In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the Super Tax liability, to the extent applicable, has already been duly discharged by our client in light of the final judicial outcome. The proposed action for further charge and recovery is therefore unwarranted and liable to be dropped in entirety.

**Issue No. __: Alleged inadmissibility of fixed expenses under section 20**

Through the subject notice, your good office has observed that, as per note 24 to the audited financial statements, our client has claimed deduction of fixed expenses amounting to Rs 1,852,228,000, and it has been alleged that such claim has been made without narrating any logical or legal basis. Accordingly, our client has been called upon to explain as to why the said amount should not be disallowed under section 20 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (the Ordinance).

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the above observation is based on a fundamental misapprehension of both the nature of the expenses and the manner in which financial statements are read. The figure referred to in the notice has been extracted from the audited financial statements; however, no specific defect, inadmissible component, or non-business element has been identified. The mere absence of a narrative explanation within the financial statements cannot, in itself, form a legal basis for disallowance.

Without prejudice to the above, it is submitted that the impugned “fixed expenses” primarily comprise **contractual fee-based charges incurred under binding commercial agreements** entered into by our client in the ordinary course of its business operations. These include payments for operational, technical, and support services which are essential for the functioning of the LNG terminal infrastructure. Such charges are not ad hoc or discretionary in nature; rather, they arise directly from enforceable contractual arrangements, duly documented and agreed between independent parties.

In substance, these expenses represent consideration for services availed and obligations performed under these agreements. The business of our client is highly structured and agreement-driven, where various operational and technical functions are outsourced or supported through specialized service providers. Accordingly, the related fee charges are an integral part of the business model and are incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of carrying on the business and generating taxable income.

It is further submitted that under section 20 of the Ordinance, the test of allowability is whether the expenditure is incurred wholly and exclusively for business purposes, unless specifically disallowed under any provision of law. In the present case, your good office has neither identified any particular expense that is capital in nature, personal in nature, or otherwise hit by any specific disallowance provision, nor has any adverse material been brought on record to suggest that these expenses lack business nexus.

The observation that no “logic or legal basis” has been provided is, with respect, misplaced. The legal basis for allowability flows directly from section 20 itself, while the factual basis lies in the underlying agreements and supporting documentation maintained by our client. If required, the same can be furnished to demonstrate the nature, purpose, and business nexus of these expenses. However, a blanket disallowance without first calling for and examining such details amounts to a generalized and unfounded presumption, which is not sustainable in law.

**In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the fixed expenses amounting to Rs 1,852,228,000 represent legitimate, agreement-backed, business-related expenditures incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of our client’s operations. The proposed disallowance under section 20, being based on assumptions rather than specific findings, is therefore unwarranted and liable to be dropped in full.**

**Issue No. __: Alleged inadmissibility of fixed expenses under section 20**

Through the subject notice, your good office has observed that, as per note 24 to the audited financial statements, our client has claimed deduction of fixed expenses amounting to Rs 1,852,228,000, and it has been alleged that such claim has been made without narrating any logical or legal basis. It is a settled position that audited financial statements, read together with notes and supporting schedules, do not—and are not required to—provide a legal justification against each individual expense line item. The purpose of financial reporting is to present a true and fair view of financial performance, whereas tax allowability is determined through application of the law to the underlying nature and purpose of the expense.

In this regard, it is submitted that the subject observation effectively constitutes a **fishing inquiry**, whereby a broad disallowance has been proposed without identifying any particular expense that is not incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of business, or which falls within the mischief of any specific disallowance provision of the Ordinance. Such an approach is not sustainable in law. Under the scheme of section 20, an expense is allowable if it is incurred wholly and exclusively for the purposes of deriving taxable income, unless it is specifically disallowed under any provision of the Ordinance. The burden, therefore, lies on the department to first identify a particular item of expense and demonstrate how it fails to meet the statutory criteria or attracts a specific prohibition.

Without prejudice to the above, it is further submitted that the so-called “fixed expenses” represent core operational costs of our client’s business. Our client operates a Floating Storage and Regasification Unit (FSRU)-based LNG terminal, being among the first LNG infrastructure projects in Pakistan. The fixed cost component in such a business model is inherently substantial and comprises expenses such as terminal operations, vessel-related charges, maintenance, technical services, and other infrastructure-linked costs that are essential for the continuous functioning of the terminal. These are not discretionary or peripheral expenses; rather, they form the backbone of the business operations and are directly and inextricably linked to the generation of revenue.

In practical terms, such expenses are akin to the fixed capacity charges in the energy sector or minimum guaranteed operational costs under long-term infrastructure arrangements. It would therefore be legally untenable to suggest, without any specific analysis, that these fundamental business expenses are not allowable under section 20. In fact, the very nature of the business necessitates incurrence of such fixed costs irrespective of volume fluctuations, and their allowability has to be examined in light of their nexus with business operations—which, in the present case, is direct and undeniable.

In absence of such identification, a blanket proposal to disallow the entire amount merely on the basis that no “logic or legal basis” has been narrated in the financial statements is not only contrary to the scheme of the Ordinance but also disregards the fundamental principle that tax disallowances must be based on concrete findings rather than generalized presumptions.

**In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the proposed disallowance of fixed expenses amounting to Rs 1,852,228,000 is based on mere assumptions, without any factual or legal foundation. The said expenses represent legitimate, wholly and exclusively incurred business expenditures, fully allowable under section 20 of the Ordinance. Accordingly, the proposed adjustment is unwarranted and liable to be dropped in entirety.**
