**Issue No. __: Alleged inadmissibility of reversal of provision for diesel**

Through the subject notice, your good office has observed that, as per note 24 to the audited financial statements, our client has claimed variable expenses amounting to Rs 2,367,451,000, and that sub-note 24.2 includes therein a reversal of provision for diesel amounting to Rs 198,432,000. On such basis, it has been alleged that deduction in respect of the said reversal would only be allowable if the corresponding provision had previously been offered to tax and, since the relevant income was exempt from tax in the earlier period, the said amount is inadmissible in terms of section 34(3) of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001. Accordingly, our client has been called upon to explain as to why the aforesaid amount should not be disallowed.

At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the very premise of the subject objection is fundamentally misconceived, both factually and legally. The amount of Rs 198,432,000 represents a **reversal of provision for diesel** and, by its very nature, is not a fresh claim, charge, or outgoing sought to be deducted from taxable income. Rather, a reversal signifies a reduction in an earlier provision and operates as a **credit** in the statement of profit or loss. In other words, it is a movement on the positive side of the accounts which reduces expense, and therefore increases accounting profit, instead of creating or enhancing any deductible expense. Consequently, the suggestion in the notice that our client has “claimed deduction” in respect of such reversal reflects a basic misreading of the accounting treatment itself.

Under the scheme of the Ordinance, expenditure is allowable, subject to the law, when it is incurred or payable under the applicable method of accounting, whereas an amount merely carried to a reserve is specifically not allowable as deduction. Section 34 provides that, under accrual basis, expenditure is incurred when the liability becomes payable, while section 21(i) expressly disallows any amount carried to a reserve fund or capitalised in any way. Thus, the statute distinguishes between an actual deductible expenditure and a reserve or provision entry. A **reversal** of such provision stands on an even clearer footing, because it does not create any deduction at all; rather, it unwinds an earlier estimate and correspondingly reduces the expense booked in the accounts. The show cause, with respect, overlooks this distinction and treats a credit adjustment as though it were a debit claim. citeturn887916view0turn130133view0

Without prejudice to the above, even the broader architecture of the Ordinance confirms that where an amount earlier allowed as deduction is subsequently recovered, reversed, or the taxpayer derives a benefit in respect thereof, the law generally addresses such later event by bringing the benefit to tax, rather than by characterising the reversal itself as an inadmissible deduction. For example, section 29(3) taxes recovery of a bad debt only where deduction had earlier been allowed, and section 30(2) similarly taxes recovery of profit on non-performing debt after prior deduction. Likewise, section 34(5A) provides that where a deduction has earlier been allowed in respect of a trading liability and the taxpayer later derives any benefit in respect of that liability, the value of such benefit is chargeable to tax in the year of receipt. These provisions make it abundantly clear that the Ordinance recognizes reversals and recoveries as potential items of **income inclusion**, subject to specific statutory conditions, and not as disallowable expenditure in the year of reversal. citeturn130133view1turn887916view0

In the present case, however, the issue does not even reach that stage, because our client has not sought any separate tax deduction on account of the impugned reversal. The reversal has merely formed part of the overall variable expense disclosure in the notes, and its effect is to reduce the expense recorded in the accounts. Therefore, if anything, the reversal already moves in favour of the Revenue by increasing accounting income. Disallowing the same once again would produce an artificial and distorted computation, as it would effectively treat a positive adjustment as though it were a negative one. Put simply, the amount in question does not reduce taxable income; hence, there is nothing capable of being “disallowed” in the first place.

Further, the observation in the notice that the earlier provision was not “offered to tax” because the income of that period was exempt is also beside the point in the present factual matrix. That line of reasoning may only arise where the taxpayer seeks deduction of an actual expense or seeks the benefit of a subsequent write-off or loss that is statutorily linked with prior taxation treatment. Here, the impugned amount is not a deduction newly claimed by our client, but merely a reversal of an earlier accounting estimate. Therefore, the alleged condition sought to be imposed in the notice has no legal application to the facts at hand.

In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the subject objection is based on a clear misapprehension of both the accounting treatment and the legal effect of the impugned entry. The reversal of provision for diesel amounting to Rs 198,432,000 is not an inadmissible deduction, nor does it constitute any claim liable to disallowance under section 34(3) or any other provision of the Ordinance. The proposed adjustment is therefore wholly unsustainable in law and on facts, and deserves to be dropped in full.

Here is a refined, technically strong response following your preferred pattern, incorporating the **client’s factual position**, addressing the **assumption of nexus**, and also bringing in the **Supreme Court principle on attribution of expenditure**:

---

**Issue No. __: Alleged disallowance of finance cost attributable to FTR income**

**7.1** Through the subject notice, your good office has observed that, as per note 28 to the audited financial statements, our client has claimed finance cost amounting to Rs 266,037,000 on account of interest/markup on long-term borrowings. It has further been alleged that the said borrowings were utilized for investment in mutual funds, the income from which falls under the Final Tax Regime (FTR). On this premise, our client has been called upon to explain as to why proportionate finance cost may not be disallowed in terms of section 28(1)(a) read with section 67 of the Income Tax Ordinance, 2001 (the Ordinance) and Rule 13 of the Income Tax Rules, 2002.

**7.2** At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the above observation is based on a mere assumption of nexus between the borrowings and the investments, without any factual verification or examination of fund flows. The notice does not identify any direct linkage demonstrating that the specific borrowed funds were utilized for making investments in mutual funds. In absence of such nexus, the proposed disallowance lacks legal foundation and amounts to a presumptive conclusion rather than a determination based on evidence.

**7.3** Without prejudice to the above, it is submitted that the long-term loan in question was obtained in 2015 at the time of commissioning of the LNG terminal and was utilized for core business purposes relating to the development and operationalization of the project. The investments in mutual funds, on the other hand, have been made out of surplus funds generated from business operations over time. Accordingly, there exists no direct or indirect nexus between the borrowed funds and the said investments.

**7.4** It is a settled principle that disallowance under section 28(1)(a) read with section 67 can only be made where a clear and demonstrable nexus exists between the expenditure and the income falling under a different regime, such as FTR. The mere existence of both borrowings and investments on the balance sheet does not, in itself, justify any apportionment. The law requires a **reasonable and evidence-based allocation**, not an assumption-based attribution.

**7.5** In this regard, reliance is placed on the settled jurisprudence, including recent pronouncements of the Honourable Supreme Court of Pakistan, wherein it has been held that **allocation or attribution of expenditure must be based on cogent material and a reasonable method, and cannot be made on arbitrary or presumptive basis**. Where the department seeks to disallow any portion of expenditure, the burden lies upon it to first establish the factual nexus and thereafter adopt a rational basis for apportionment. In absence of such exercise, any proposed disallowance is not sustainable.

**7.6** It is further submitted that Rule 13 of the Income Tax Rules, 2002 also contemplates allocation of expenditure only where the same is **common and attributable** to multiple streams of income. In the present case, the finance cost relates to long-term project financing, whereas the investments have been made independently out of internally generated funds. Therefore, the condition of “common attributable expenditure” is not satisfied in the first place.

**7.7** In view of the foregoing, it is respectfully submitted that the proposed disallowance of proportionate finance cost is based on an incorrect presumption of fund utilization, without any factual or legal basis. The finance cost has been incurred wholly and exclusively for business purposes and bears no nexus with income falling under FTR. Accordingly, the proposed adjustment is unwarranted and liable to be dropped in entirety.  

---

Here is a refined and more focused version, keeping it **crisp, commercially grounded, and less abstract**, while incorporating your key points on **FSRU rentals, time charter basis, and absence of any benchmarking or market challenge**:

---

**5.1** Through the subject notice, your good office has observed that, as per note No. 24 to the audited financial statements, our client has claimed deduction of fixed expenses amounting to Rs 1,852,228,000, and it has been alleged that such claim has been made without narrating any logical or legal basis. On this premise, our client has been called upon to show cause as to why the said amount should not be disallowed under section 20 of the Ordinance.  

**5.2** At the outset, it is respectfully submitted that the above observation is general in nature and is not supported by any specific defect or adverse material. The amount has merely been picked from the audited financial statements without examining the underlying nature of the expense. Financial statements are not intended to provide legal justification against each line item; rather, allowability under tax law is determined based on the nature and purpose of the expense, which in the present case has not been questioned with any specificity.  

**5.3** The impugned observation effectively amounts to a fishing inquiry, as no particular expense has been identified as being non-business, capital in nature, or otherwise inadmissible. Under section 20, an expense is allowable if it is incurred wholly and exclusively for business purposes, unless specifically disallowed. A blanket proposal to disallow an entire category of expenses, without identifying any defect, falls outside the settled principles governing such proceedings.  

**5.4** Without prejudice to the above, it is submitted that the so-called “fixed expenses” primarily represent **FSRU rental charges and related contractual payments**, incurred under a duly executed agreement on a **time charter basis**. These payments are not arbitrary or discretionary; rather, they are governed by binding contractual terms, determined with reference to internationally prevailing commercial practices for such specialized assets. The FSRU being a critical operational asset, the associated rental expense constitutes a fundamental cost of running the business and is directly linked to revenue generation.  

**5.5** It is further submitted that your good office has neither questioned the commercial terms of the agreement nor invoked any benchmarking, comparability, or market-based analysis to suggest that the expense is excessive or unreasonable. In absence of any such exercise, the proposed disallowance appears to be based purely on assumptions and presumptions, without any reference to actual market conditions or contractual realities.  

**5.6** In these circumstances, it is respectfully submitted that the expenses in question are clearly incurred in the normal course of business, are agreement-backed, and have a direct nexus with the operations of our client. No element of capital, personal, or non-business nature has been identified to justify disallowance under section 20.  

**5.7** In view of the foregoing, the proposed disallowance of fixed expenses amounting to Rs 1,852,228,000 is without any factual or legal basis and is liable to be dropped in entirety.  

---

10. **That the order suffers from factual inaccuracies and computational errors**, which have materially impacted the assessed income and tax liability.

the DCIR has erred in recovering FED without considering that after the 18th Amendment to the Constitution of Pakistan, taxing services has become a provincial matter. Any federal tax or duty on services is unlawful. The SHC has ruled that the FED Act, concerning taxable services within the Provincial domain, is ultra vires the Constitution effective July 1, 2011. The ATIR in the case of PAKSAT International (Private) Limited vide order in STA No. 182/KB/2015 dated February 16, 2016 has ruled that the after the promulgation of SSTSA with effect from July 1, 2011, the taxation officer of FBR does not have the jurisdiction to initiate any proceeding to recover tax on services (which are presently covered by the provincial laws) even in respect of periods prior to promulgation of the SSTSA.
items.title: FED Jurisdiction After 18th Amendment

ریکارڈ چیک کریں، ہم نے اس کے سٹرچ ورک گراؤنڈز بنائے تھے، وہ گراؤنڈس چیک کریں

**Subject:** Appeal before Tribunal – Reverse Charge Mechanism | Way Forward

Dear Omer,

I hope you are doing well.

As you are aware, your appeals before the Tribunal in respect of the Reverse Charge Mechanism were fixed last week. During the course of the hearings, we have duly presented and concluded our arguments before the Honorable Bench.

In this regard, it is important to highlight that a recent judgment by the entity["organization","Supreme Court of Pakistan","Pakistan apex court"] has upheld the validity of the Reverse Charge Mechanism. This development significantly impacts the legal position of the matter and, from a legal standpoint, there appears to be limited room to sustain the appeal going forward.

Further, from a factual perspective, it is pertinent to note that the major component of the input tax relating to the relevant period had already been claimed in Tax Year 2020. Subsequently, during departmental proceedings initiated under Section 11, the matter was addressed, and the position was regularized—both in terms of payment and validation of input tax adjustments by the department.

Given the above, there appears to be no practical avenue available to pursue this matter further. Even if the case is continued on legal grounds and a favorable outcome is achieved, it would lead to a commercially and procedurally impractical position. Specifically, it would raise questions such as whether a refund may be pursued before SRB while corresponding payments would be required under FBR, which does not present a viable or beneficial outcome. Moreover, there is no clear mechanism available under the Sindh sales tax framework to effectively claim and realize such refunds in these circumstances.

In light of the overall legal and factual position, and considering the practical constraints involved, our preliminary view is that continuation of the appeal may not yield any tangible benefit.

We would, however, appreciate your perspective on the matter before taking any final position. For your information, there is also some pressure from the department to either withdraw or not press the appeal; however, we will evaluate that aspect separately. At this stage, we wanted to clearly present our assessment and seek your input on the appropriate way forward.

We look forward to your guidance.

Kind regards,  
[Your Name]

اچھا ایک ای میل ڈرافٹ کریں انگریش اس کا نام یہ بولیں کہ ہائی کومر، ایز یو آر وئیر کہ آپ کی جو ہے اپیلز بفر ٹریبونل آن ریورس چارج میکنیزم فکس ہوئی تھی لاسٹ ویک، ڈورنگ دا ہیرنگز ہم نے اپنے سارے ارگومنٹس جو ہے فڈنس کر دی ہیں بیفور دا کورٹ اور اس میں آپ ایک اور چیز یہ بتا دیں کہ ریسنٹلی سپریم کورٹ کا ججمنٹ آیا ہے جس کے اندر اس نے ریورس چارج میکنیزم کو الٹا ورش سے ویلیڈ کر دی ہے، ٹھیک ہے؟ اب اور اس کا مطلب یہ ہے کہ آپ کے اس میں کوئی لیگل پوائنٹ آف ویو سے کوئی انفارمیشنز ایگزسٹ نہیں کرتے اچھا اور کیپنگ ان ویو آف فیکچول پوائنٹس کہ جو جو اس سال کے یعنی کہ جو میجر کمپوننٹ ہے آپ کا جو ان پٹ ٹیکس کا وہ آپ نے ٹونٹی کے اندر کلیم کیا تھا جو کہ ہم نے ڈپارٹمنٹل پروسیڈنگز میں سیکشن گیارہ کے جو نوٹس آئے تھے اس کے اندر ہم نے ردوبی کرا دیا یعنی کہ اس کی پیمنٹ بھی ہو گئی اس کی ان پٹ ٹیکس کی ایجسٹمنٹ بھی ڈپارٹمنٹ میں ویلیڈیٹ کر دی ہے تو اب کوئی ایونیو ہمارے نظر میں بچتا نہیں ہے کہ اس کو آگے کنٹینیو لے کے چلنے کا آن دا لیگل فرنٹ بھی کیونکہ اگر لیگل ایلی بھی ہم اس کو آگے لے کے چلتے ہیں تو کیا ہم ان دا فیورول آؤٹکم ہم کیا ایس آر بی کے اندر ریفنڈ فائل کریں گے اور ایف بی آر پہ پیمنٹ کریں گے تو وہ بھی ہمارے لیے بینیفیشل نہیں ہے یہ تمام چیزیں تو اس چیزوں کو مدنظر رکھتے ہوئے ہم کہیں گے آپ اپنا تھوڑا سا سٹاپ پوائنٹ آف ویو ہم سے شیئر کریں کہ ہم کیونکہ ہمیں تھوڑا سا ڈپارٹمنٹل کی طرف سے ایک پریس آ رہا ہے کہ یا تو آپ اپیل کو ویڈڈروا کریں یا نوٹ پرس کریں ہاویور ہم اس کو تو دیکھ لیں گے لیکن ہم اپنا پوائنٹ آف ویو آپ کو کلیئر کرنا چاہ رہے تھے کہ اس اپیل کا ویسے بھی کوئی فیکٹ نہیں ہے کیونکہ اس کا جو جو ہم جو فیکچول بینیفٹ ہے وہ آلریڈی ہم اویل کر چکے ہیں اگر ہم لیگل فرنٹ پہ جاتے بھی ہیں اور فارچونزیک میں ہمارے فیور میں بھی آ جاتا ہے تو فیکچولی ہم کافی کنفیوز پوزیشن پہ ارائو ہو جائیں گے کہ ہم کیا ایس آر بی کو پیمنٹ کریں گے اور ایس آر بی میں ریفنڈ فائل کریں گے کیونکہ کوئی ہمیں پروویجن نظر نہیں آتا ایس آر بی کے اندر اس طرح کا ریفنڈ کلیم کا اور وہ دیں گے بھی نہیں تو اس کو دیکھتے ہوئے کیپنگ ان ویو آل دا سرکمسٹینسز آپ اپنا پوائنٹ آف ویو ہمیں شیئر کریں

:::writing{variant="email" id="94821" subject="Closure of Remand Proceedings – Disallowed Input Tax on Blacklisted Purchases"}
Dear Sir,

We hope you are doing well.

As you are aware, while processing your pending sales tax refunds in prior years, the tax department had disallowed a relatively small portion of input tax on the grounds of purchases made from blacklisted vendors. Against this disallowance, we had initially filed an appeal before the Commissioner (Appeals).

Subsequently, the learned Commissioner (Appeals), without providing an adequate opportunity of being heard, remanded the matter back to the department for re-examination. Pursuant to this, remand proceedings were initiated by the department, and over the years we have been consistently seeking extensions in order to compile the required supporting documentation.

However, it is pertinent to highlight that the disallowance pertains to miscellaneous vendors for which detailed records, particularly invoice-wise breakups and supporting documentation, are not available at your end. Given the absence of these critical records, it is not practically feasible to substantiate the claim or pursue a meaningful resolution in the remand proceedings.

It is also important to note that this matter strictly relates to the refund claim and does not impact your current input tax adjustments, which have already been duly claimed and processed in subsequent periods. Furthermore, the relevant tax periods are quite old, relating to times when manual returns were filed, and therefore retrieval of complete documentation is no longer viable.

In view of the above, continuing with these remand proceedings would not yield any substantive outcome and would only result in further administrative effort without benefit. Accordingly, we seek your approval to formally close/withdraw these proceedings and avoid pursuing further extensions.

We look forward to your confirmation in this regard.

Best regards,  
[Your Name]
:::

اچھا ایک ای میل ڈرافٹ کریں ہائوکامر ایز یو آر ایئر کہ جب ہم نے آپ کے سیل ٹیکس کے پینڈنگ ریفنڈس پروسس کروائے تھے تو فرام ویریئس ٹیکس فیلڈ ڈپارٹمنٹ نے ایک بہت ہی اسمالر اماؤنٹ کو انڈر لیو آف بلیکلسٹڈ پرچیزز ان پوٹ ٹیکس ہمارے ڈسالاؤ کیا تھا اس کو ہم نے انیشللی کمیشنر اپیلس پہ اپیل فائل کر دی تھی ٹھیک ہے اور پھر کمشنر اپیلس نے انڈر ریسٹ آپ نے اوپورچونٹی نہیں دی اور اس طرح ہماری بات کو ریمانڈ کر دیا تھا اچھا اب وہ ہم کافی عرصے سے یہ ریمانڈ پروسیڈنگ جو ہے وہ ڈپارٹمنٹ نے انشیئٹ کی ہیں اور ہم بیک ٹو بیک ایکسٹینشنز اس میں فائل کر رہے ہیں کیونکہ اس میں ہمارے پاس کوئی ڈیٹیلز فرام یور اینٹ ہیں نہیں ٹھیک ہے کیونکہ یہ سارے انمیشنلینیس وینڈرز ہیں جن کا کوئی ڈیٹیل کوئی ریکارڈ ہمارے پاس انوائس وائس بریک اپ ہے نہیں تو اس پہ اوور رولنگ جو ہے وہ نہیں ہو سکتی ٹھیک ہے کیونکہ ریفنڈ کے لیے ہمیں یہ جو ہے نا ریفنڈ کے لیے ہمیں اس کے انوائسز اور اس طرح کی اوور رولنگز ریکوائر ہے یہ اس کو اس میٹر کو ان پوٹ ٹیکس ایڈجسٹمنٹ سے لنک نہیں کرے گا جس میں آلریڈی ویریئس ایڈجسٹمٹس موجود ہیں کہ ان پوٹ ٹیکس آپ کو دینا ہے لیکن یہ پیریڈ بھی بہت پرانے پرانے ہیں اس میں ایئر ویر بھی نہیں ہوتا تھا بلکہ مینول ریٹن ہوتا تھا تو وہ پروسیڈنگ یہاں پہ نہیں آپ کی سسٹین کرتی تو انشار یہ ہے کہ ہم آپ سے اس کا اپروول چاہ رہے ہیں کہ ہم اس پروسیڈنگز کو ختم کریں کیونکہ ہمارے پاس کوئی ڈیٹیل نہیں ہے اور ریڈیجیکٹڈ ہے اور تاکہ ہم اس کو فڈرر ایکسٹینشنز میں نہ لائیں کیونکہ اس میں ہم نے بہت یعنی کہ اوور دی ایئرز ہم ایکسٹینشنز میں فائل کر رہے ہیں اور ہمارے پاس کوئی ڈیٹیل بھی نہیں ہے اس کی ایک ای میل مجھے ڈرافٹ کر کے دے دیں

Understood — I’ve incorporated your exact positioning, especially the distinction between **pre-amendment vs post-Finance Act 2025 regime**, and framed it in a clear, technically sound manner.

You can send the following:

---

:::writing{variant="email" id="59382" subject="RE: FW: WEPL WHT challan Invoice Ref No. HBLJanToOct-2025"}
Hi Hashim,

We have reviewed the response shared by HBL and the overall position requires to be evaluated in light of the evolving legal framework, particularly in Sindh.

At the outset, it is important to note that the entire controversy around levy of sales tax on renting of immovable property historically arose under the earlier legal regime, where reliance was placed on the judgment in the case of entity["legal_case","Young's case","SHC decision on renting of immovable property taxation"]. This position was subsequently reaffirmed by the Sindh High Court and also attained finality at the level of the entity["organization","Supreme Court of Pakistan","apex court of Pakistan"].

However, the legal position in Sindh has materially evolved since then. The Sindh Finance Act, 2025 introduced further amendments, and the matter has now effectively entered a **third phase of the law**, where the statutory framework governing taxation of renting of immovable property has been revisited.

In this context, the following points are relevant:

• The earlier judicial precedents (including Young’s case) relate to the **pre-amendment legal regime**. Their applicability to the amended law is not automatic and needs to be examined separately.  
• For the **post-Finance Act 2025 period**, the taxability position must be evaluated independently under the amended provisions.  
• If any taxpayer (including banks) has challenged the amended provisions before the Sindh High Court and has obtained a **specific interim relief / stay order covering the amended law**, then reliance on such relief may be considered — but only to the extent it is clearly applicable to the relevant period and jurisdiction.  
• In the absence of a valid and operative stay covering the amended regime, the default position would be to follow the law as it currently stands, including applicability of Sindh sales tax (currently at 3%) on renting of immovable property.

Accordingly, from WEPL’s perspective, it would be important to first ascertain whether HBL is relying on:

(i) judicial precedents under the **old law**, or  
(ii) any **fresh petition/stay obtained after the Finance Act 2025 amendments**.

Only in the latter case, and subject to verification of the scope of such interim relief, can a view be taken to not charge SST on rent for the relevant period.

As regards Punjab, the position is comparatively clear since the levy on renting of immovable property has already been withdrawn through the relevant notification, and therefore no such exposure exists there.

In view of the above, we recommend that HBL may be requested to provide a copy of any **post-amendment petition and interim relief**, if being relied upon. Based on that, an informed decision can be taken on the appropriate treatment going forward.

For prior periods (i.e., pre-amendment), the matter would need to be evaluated separately in light of the earlier legal regime and may require independent handling.

Please let us know if you would like us to draft a response to HBL accordingly.

Best regards,  
Zuhair
:::

---

If you want, I can also prepare a **more assertive version** pushing HBL to either pay SST or formally indemnify WEPL — which is usually the safer commercial position in these cases.

Subject: RE: WEPL WHT challan Invoice Ref No. HBLJanToOct-2025

 

Hi @Basheer, Jannat WEP-DRR/B/68

 

Pls. find our concerned team response for your ready reference on SST.

 

The Banking industry is collectively of the view that renting of immovable property does not constitute a service.

 

There have been some architectural changes in provincial sales tax laws w.e.f. July 1, 2025 which had an effect of making rent taxable (the reason why OMCs are charging sales tax on rent). After these changes, Banks approached Council of Common Interest (CCI) without any positive outcome and many banks have also recently filed petitions before Islamabad High Court which are pending and hence the matter remains contentious.

 

Apparently in view of the evident issues with (incorrectly) taxing rent as well as remarks of Rawalpindi Bench of Lahore High Court in a related case, Punjab Revenue Authority (PRA) notified rent on immoveable property as tax free (notification attached effective Oct 22, 2025)). Now this is a relief, but fundamentally, Banks do not even consider rent as a service, let alone taxable or non-taxable. Without prejudice to this, the notification at least accepts the issue and addresses the concerns, though in a manner not deemed entirely correct

 

Moreover, Peshawar High Court has also granted a conditional stay in relation to the matter (dated Oct 15, 2025).

 

Lastly, a judgment of Supreme Court is also attached, where the apex Court spoke its mind as well, while agreeing with an earlier SHC judgment.

 

Based on the above, we are of the view that charging sales tax on rent (which has historically been a contentious issue) without exhausting legal options is not fundamentally the right approach. In case OMCs have a conflicting view, please do share with us backed with legal opinion/reasoning.

 

Muhammad Kamran                                            

Relationship Manager

Below is a polished response you can send to Hashim. I have aligned it with the current position under Sindh law and the reported court position on taxability of mere rent of immovable property. The key point is that HBL’s position is arguable in law, but from WEPL’s practical perspective the matter should be handled contractually and commercially as well, not only technically. Sindh’s law was amended through the Sindh Finance Act, 2025, and the updated Sindh statute now specifically deals with recovery/payment of tax on renting of immovable property. At the same time, the Sindh High Court in *Young’s* held that mere renting of immovable property is not a taxable service, and that position has been noted again by the Sindh High Court in 2025, including reference to the Supreme Court’s 5 September 2022 judgment maintaining *Young’s* and dismissal of the review on 11 January 2024. Punjab separately inserted a tax-free entry on 22 October 2025 for supply of immovable property by way of lease, licence or similar arrangement. citeturn130529search0turn130529search5turn299277view4turn299277view5turn406443search0turn406443search6

You can send the following:

:::writing{variant="email" id="48126" subject="RE: FW: WEPL WHT challan Invoice Ref No. HBLJanToOct-2025"}
Hi Hashim,

We have reviewed the below exchange.

At a high level, HBL’s stance is based on the long-standing judicial controversy around levy of provincial sales tax on mere renting of immovable property. In Sindh, the Sindh High Court in *Young’s* had held that mere letting out of immovable property by a landlord to a tenant does not involve provision of a taxable service, and this position has subsequently been noted again by the Sindh High Court in a later reported matter as having been maintained by the Supreme Court. Accordingly, HBL’s view is not without legal basis.

That said, the matter cannot be looked at only from HBL’s side. From WEPL’s perspective, if WEPL has issued a tax invoice charging Sindh sales tax and has correspondingly treated the amount as tax collectible/payable in its sales tax compliance, non-recovery from HBL may still leave WEPL commercially exposed unless the position is contractually and compliantly regularized. In other words, even where taxability is contentious, the vendor should avoid a situation where output tax is reported or becomes payable but remains unrecovered from the customer.

Further, Sindh law was amended through the Sindh Finance Act, 2025 and the updated Sindh statute now contains specific provisions dealing with payment/recovery of tax on renting of immovable property. Therefore, while the judicial controversy remains relevant, it would not be advisable for WEPL to rely only on pre-amendment case law without first reconciling the current statutory framework, WEPL’s invoicing/tax reporting position, and the contractual tax clause with HBL.

In our view, the practical way forward would be as follows:

1. WEPL should first check whether the relevant invoice has already been declared in the Sindh sales tax return as a taxable supply and whether any output tax has already been paid or is payable in relation to the same.
2. The underlying agreement with HBL should be reviewed carefully, especially the tax gross-up / tax over-and-above / tax inclusive wording. If the contract clearly provides that applicable indirect taxes are recoverable from HBL over and above rent, WEPL has a stronger commercial footing to insist on payment unless HBL furnishes a clear legal cover.
3. HBL may be asked to share complete copies of the documents it is relying upon, including the alleged stay order and the judgment(s), since their email only makes a general reference to those proceedings.
4. Subject to review of the contract and WEPL’s actual sales tax reporting, WEPL may respond that:
   - WEPL acknowledges that the matter is under litigation and remains contentious;
   - however, unless HBL provides a specific and operative order covering the relevant levy / period / jurisdiction, WEPL is constrained to follow its current invoicing and compliance position;
   - accordingly, HBL should either pay the invoiced Sindh sales tax or provide documentary legal basis enabling WEPL to revise its tax treatment without exposure.
5. If commercially feasible, a without prejudice middle ground may also be discussed, whereby HBL pays the principal rent and either:
   - pays the SST under protest; or
   - the disputed SST amount is parked / withheld pending final legal determination, but only after WEPL confirms that its own tax reporting can be aligned accordingly.

So, in summary, I would not recommend that WEPL simply concede HBL’s position at this stage. HBL’s legal argument is arguable, but WEPL should take a position only after confirming (i) the contract wording, (ii) WEPL’s Sindh sales tax reporting for the invoice, and (iii) the exact scope of the stay/order being relied upon by HBL.

If helpful, we can also prepare a short draft response back to HBL on these lines.

Best regards,  
Zuhair
:::
